papers.version_note: arXiv:2410.17471v1, 22 Oct 2024. The text layer lost the math symbols of Eqs. (1) and (2) (printed as unreadable glyphs); the surrounding prose was read in full. Figures 1 to 5 are images; only their captions are in the text layer, so the confusion-matrix entries are not read.
papers.what_it_is: A Stevens Institute of Technology experiment that classifies 1000 MNIST digits from the first detected photon through ten Hermite-Gaussian mode projections and reports 31.00% fidelity against a 24.57% simulated single-pixel classical classifier.

assertions.value: The authors define first photon machine learning as a task in which only one photon-detection event is allowed per pattern and the digit class must be inferred after that first photon is detected.
quotes: For each pattern, only one photon-detection event is allowed, where its digit class (i.e., label) must be inferred after the first photon is detected, hence the name of first photon machine learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own task in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that each image is a standard binary pattern with 28 × 28 pixels from the MNIST handwritten digit set, encoded as the spatial modes of a few-photon coherent signal through a binary spatial modulator with on/off pixels.
quotes: each image is a standard binary pattern with 28 × 28 pixels from the MNIST handwritten digit set.
The patterns are encoded as the spatial modes of a few-photon coherent signal through a binary spatial modulator with on/off pixels.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own input format in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experiment uses the first 100 handwritten patterns of each digit in the MNIST library, which gives 1000 patterns in total.
quotes: we consider the first 100 hand-written patterns of each digit in the MNIST library, so that the total pattern number is 1000.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the size of its own test set in Section 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The result covers 1000 training-set digits and no held-out or full MNIST test set, so the 31.00% figure is for this subset only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classical classifier (CC) and the quantum classifier (QC) use the same resources to recognize the same patterns under the same constraint, that classification is made on detection of the very first photon, and that the only difference is that quantum superposition is used in QC but not permitted in CC.
quotes: the two use the same resources to recognize the same patterns under the same constraint: the classification is made upon the detection of the very first photon.
The only difference, however, is that the effect of quantum superposition is utilized in QC, but not permitted in CC.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the design of its own comparison in Section 2.
assertions.reader_inference: The CC arm is evaluated as a calculation on the same 1000 patterns, not run in hardware (see the separate assertion on the CC method).

assertions.value: The authors state that Fischbacher and Sbaiz proved the optimum classical classifier first identifies the pixel from which the detected photon comes and then assigns each pixel its most likely label, that no method including redistributing light intensity among pixels can exceed the resulting accuracy threshold, and that the threshold is 22.96% for the whole MNIST handwritten data set against 10% for random guessing.
quotes: Fischbacher and Sbaiz proved that the optimum classifier is realized by first identifying the pixel from which the detected photon comes, and then determining for each pixel what the most likely label is (49).
No method, including redistributing light intensity among pixels, can help exceed this threshold.
For the whole MNIST handwritten data set, the accuracy threshold is 22.96%, which is significantly higher than that by random guessing (10%).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the classical optimum to Fischbacher and Sbaiz and does not reprove it.
assertions.reader_inference: The 22.96% bound is quoted for the whole MNIST set, while the experiment uses 1000 patterns; the paper's own CC calculation on those 1000 patterns gives 24.57%, above 22.96%.

assertions.value: The authors state that Fischbacher and Sbaiz found a classifier using quantum superposition can theoretically achieve an accuracy above 41.27%, and that no experimental implementation was proposed in that work.
quotes: a classifier utilizing quantum superposition can theoretically achieve an accuracy above 41.27%, although no experimental implementation was proposed.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result from other work; the paper does not reprove it.
assertions.reader_inference: The measured 31.00% lies between the classical bound and this quantum bound.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing the same prior work, that any transformation is permitted in the classical case but it will not help increase the fidelity.
quotes: Note that any transformation is permitted in the classical case, but it won’t help increase the fidelity (49).
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result; the conditions are not restated in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the classical case the which-way information is revealed so the transmitted photons are in an incoherent mixture state, whereas in the quantum case the photon takes multiple paths without knowing which and is in a pure state with nonzero off-diagonal terms in the density matrix.
quotes: The only difference is that in the classical case, the “which way” information is revealed, so that the transmitted photons is in an incoherent mixture state:
giving nonzero off-diagonal terms in density matrix (2).
assertions.certainty_reason: A simplified description given by the authors, with the text layer losing the equations.
assertions.reader_inference: The input light is a weak coherent laser beam, so the pure-state description is that of a coherent state in a spatial mode, as the authors write for both arms.

assertions.value: The authors state that the physics behind the quantum classifier is identical to the double-slit experiment, with each pixel viewed as a slit.
quotes: The physics behind QC is thus identical to that behind the double-slit experiment (39), where
assertions.certainty_reason: An analogy stated without derivation in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors state that in this experiment the photons are projected onto 10 spatial modes, one per digit class, so that no further data processing is required and the entire neural network is implemented in the optics domain.
quotes: In this experiment, we consider the simplest case where the photons are projected onto 10 spatial modes.
In this way, no further data processing is required, and the entire neural network is implemented in the optics domain.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own readout design in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors describe the setup as a femtosecond mode-locked laser producing probe (1554 nm) and pump (1564 nm) pulse trains, a digital micromirror device (DMD) that encodes the MNIST patterns, a liquid crystal spatial light modulator (SLM) that imprints 10 phase masks one per label, a periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide for frequency upconversion quantum parametric mode sorting, and a silicon single-photon detector.
quotes: generate the probe (1554 nm) and pump (1564 nm) pulse trains.
The DMD is used to encode the MNIST patterns onto the photons, while the SLM is used to imprint onto the photons 10 phase masks, each for one of the 10 labels.
waveguide for frequency upconversion quantum parametric mode sorting (52–55).
The upconverted signal is detected by a silicon single-photon detector
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own apparatus in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the setup combines spatial light modulation with quantum parametric mode sorting (QPMS) to ensure mode-projective measurement with high purity, and that the single-mode fiber coupling efficiency is about 40% before any modulation is applied.
quotes: whose coupling efficiency is about 40% before any modulation is applied either by the DMD or SLM.
This setup combines spatial light modulation for high dimensional information coding and quantum parametric mode sorting (QPMS) to ensure mode-projective measurement with high purity.
assertions.certainty_reason: The mode-purity claim is stated without a measured value in the text read; the 40% figure is a setup parameter.
assertions.reader_inference: No measured mode purity or crosstalk figure appears in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 10 phase masks are uploaded on the SLM one after another while the reflected photons are collected in the single-mode fiber and detected, and that the rotation stops when the first photon detection is registered and the pattern is assigned to the corresponding label.
quotes: Then, the 10 phase masks are sequentially uploaded on the SLM screen while the reflected
The rotation stops when the first photon detection is registered, and the pattern is assigned to the corresponding label.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own measurement procedure in Section 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The ten modes are tested one at a time in time sequence on one photon stream; the label is the mask on display at the first detection, not a single simultaneous 10-way measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the SLM refresh rate is about 0.7 frames per second, that each SLM mask takes about 1.4 seconds, and that each digit pattern therefore takes at least 14 seconds, with the actual time much longer.
quotes: Limited mainly by the low refreshing rate of the SLM (about 0.7 frames per second), the total time to complete the measurement for each SLM mask is about 1.4 seconds, so that it takes at least 14 seconds to finish each digit pattern
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this time limit of their own apparatus in Section 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's speed claim in the abstract and the conclusion is a prospect; the demonstrated throughput is slower than 14 seconds per image.

assertions.value: The authors state that the probe power was set so that at most 0.1 photon is detected per pulse, and that for the MNIST digits the detected photon number per pulse is between 0.001 and 0.06 on average.
quotes: Then, we use the VA to adjust the probe power level so that at most 0.1 photon is detected per pulse.
For the MNIST digits, the detected photon number per pulse is between 0.001 and 0.06 on average.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own operating regime in Section 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The run is a many-pulse weak-coherent experiment filtered to the first detection, not a deterministic single-photon source.

assertions.value: The authors state that for each label they chose a Hermite-Gaussian mode that gives the highest Bayesian probability for that label when a photon is detected in it, restricted their choices to a dozen Hermite-Gaussian modes without much optimization, and first selected HG11,4, HG5,3, HG5,11, HG4,7, HG11,3, HG8,13, HG6,4, H13,4, HG8,3 and HG12,13 for Label 0 to 9.
quotes: For each label, we choose a Hermite-Gaussian (HG) mode such that when it is on display and a photon is detected, the Bayesian probability of the digit pattern under test in this label is the highest among all labels.
we restrict our choices to a dozen of Hermite Gaussian modes, in hope to show that even without much optimization,
we first select HG11,4, HG5,3, HG5,11, HG4,7, HG11,3, HG8,13, HG6,4, H13,4, HG8,3, and HG12,13 for Label 0 to 9, respectively
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own mode choice in Section 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The modes were chosen from the same 1000 patterns that were then classified, so the mode selection and the test set are not separate.

assertions.value: The authors report an average fidelity for all labels of 31.00% ± 0.77% for the experimental quantum classifier, with the uncertainty calculated from the shot-noise statistics of photon counting, from two rounds of measurements.
quotes: The average fidelity for all labels in 31.00% ± 0.77%, where the uncertainty is calculated based on the shot-noise statistics of photon counting.
where two rounds of measurements are carried out.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical result from one study on 1000 patterns.
assertions.reader_inference: The stated uncertainty is shot noise only; it does not include variation from the choice of patterns or masks.

assertions.value: The authors report that every label has a success probability well above 0.1 of random guess, that the highest fidelity is 42% for Label 0 and the lowest is 18% for Label 2, and that all labels except Label 2 have the highest probability of being correctly classified.
quotes: For all labels, the success probability is well above 0.1 of random guess.
The highest fidelity is 42%, achieved for Label “0”, and lowest is 18% for Label 2.
Except for Label 2, all labels have the highest probability of being corrected classified.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the matrix entries are in a figure image.

assertions.value: The authors state that the ideal classical classifier is a thought-experiment calculation: for each label one index pixel is chosen to give the highest Bayesian probability, a pattern is assigned with equal probability to the labels whose index pixels it contains, and a pattern with no index pixel is assigned to any of the 10 labels with 1/10 probability each.
quotes: As a comparison, Fig. 4 shows the thought-experiment results for the ideal CC.
Then, we assign the pattern with equal probability to the labels those pixels indicate.
In rare cases when a pattern contains no index pixel, then it will be assigned to any of the 10 labels, each with 1/10 probability.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its own classical comparison is computed in Section 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical figure is a calculation, not a measurement made with the same optical hardware, detector noise or loss.

assertions.value: The authors state that the index pixels chosen for the ten labels in order have coordinates (12,18), (14,13), (15,14), (14,14), (19,12), (12,11), (13,15), (8,16), (15,10) and (15,15), and that they distribute around the center regime where the information-carrying features are mostly located.
quotes: As seen, those pixels distribute around the center regime, where the information-carrying features are mostly located.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the pixels used for its own classical comparison in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors report for the ideal classical classifier a highest accuracy of 49% for Label 0, a lowest of 17% for Label 8, and an average over all labels of 24.57%, which they describe as close to the theoretical threshold for all pixels and all patterns.
quotes: the highest accuracy of 49% is achieved for Label “0”, and the lowest of 17% is achieved for Label “8”.
The average over all labels is 24.57%, close to the theoretical threshold for all pixels and all patterns (49, 59).
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation result from one study on 1000 patterns.
assertions.reader_inference: 24.57% is above the 22.96% bound quoted for the whole MNIST set, so the classical reference on this subset is a little above the cited bound, and the abstract rounds it to about 24%.

assertions.value: The authors state that QC clearly outperforms CC, with a classification fidelity of 31.00% against 24.57%, and that this exhibits an unambiguous advantage originating from the quantum superposition principle.
quotes: Comparing the results in Figs. 4 and 3, QC clearly outperforms CC, whose classification fidelity of 31.00% is significantly higher than 24.57%.
This exhibits an unambiguous advantage originating from the quantum superposition principle.
assertions.certainty_reason: The author's own interpretation of one experiment against one calculation.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is an experiment (weak coherent light, 1000 patterns, mode set tuned on those patterns) against a calculated single-pixel classifier. The paper gives no statistical test for the gap and no classical wave-optics baseline that also uses coherent light, so whether this is a quantum advantage rather than a coherent-optics effect is the authors' interpretation, not a tested result.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that a single photon can perform image recognition at around 30% fidelity, which beats by a large margin the theoretical limit of what a similar classical system can possibly achieve (about 24%).
quotes: our experiment finds that a single photon can perform image recognition at around 30% fidelity, which beats by a large margin the theoretical limit of what a similar classical system can possibly achieve (about 24%).
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract's summary of one study's result.
assertions.reader_inference: The body gives 31.00% for the main run and 30.00% and 29.95% for the two other mode sets; the 24% reference is the paper's own calculation on 1000 patterns.

assertions.value: The authors state that the advantage is only in the sense of a statistical average, that it does not imply the current QC is advantageous for every pattern or class, and that the ideal CC obtains higher accuracy for Label 0.
quotes: We note, however, that this advantage is only in the sense of statistical average.
In fact, in the present results, higher classification accuracies are obtained with the ideal CC for Label “0”.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit on their own result in Section 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The per-label figures stated in the text (QC 42% and CC 49% for Label 0) agree with this.

assertions.value: The authors state that CC samples only a particular pixel of the patterns while QC samples all pixels simultaneously and probes the correlation among them through interference measurement, which they say suits capturing holistic features.
quotes: This is because CC only samples a particular pixel of the patterns.
In contrast, QC samples simultaneously all pixels; in fact, it probes the correlation among those pixels through interference measurement.
it is advantageous in capturing the wholistic features, similar to how visual information is processed in eyes.
assertions.certainty_reason: An explanation offered by the authors without a test in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors state that the comparison is between the theoretical results of an ideal CC and the experimental results of an under-optimized QC, and claim that the observed advantage is not specific to the particular patterns or phase masks they chose.
quotes: the above comparison is made between the theoretical results of an ideal CC and experimental results of an under-optimized QC.
The observed advantage is not specific to the particular patterns or phase masks we choose.
assertions.certainty_reason: The first sentence is the authors' statement of the basis of their own comparison; the second is a claim.
assertions.reader_inference: The generality claim rests on two further mode sets on the same 1000 patterns, not on other datasets or tasks.

assertions.value: The authors report that two other sets of Hermite-Gaussian modes give classification fidelities of 30.00%±1.14% and 29.95%±0.93%, similar to the main run.
quotes: The the classification fidelities are 30.00%±1.14% and 29.95%±0.93%, respectively, similar to Fig.3.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: From the mode lists in the text, set (a) differs from the main set by replacing HG8,3 with HG3,4, and set (b) by replacing HG5,3 with HG5,4, so each changes one mode; this tests sensitivity to a single mode, not a different design.

assertions.value: The authors state that the decision is made on detection of a single photon whose energy is merely 10−19 joule, that the equivalent energy per calculation is much less than 10−24 joule, or about 10−6 photons, which they say is orders of magnitude lower than the state of the art.
quotes: the decision is made upon the detection of a single photon, whose energy is merely 10−19 joule.
The equivalent energy consumption per calculation is much less than 10−24 joule, or about 10−6 photons, which is orders of magnitude lower than the state of the art (48).
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the text read does not show the derivation of the per-calculation figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The derivation of the per-calculation figure, including how many calculations one photon is counted as, is not in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors state that although only a single photon is detected for the decision, the whole system energy consumption is much more than 10−19 when the power for optical and electronic devices and emitted but undetected photons is counted, and that further reduction will require replacing electronics with optics.
quotes: we would like to point out that although only a single photon is detected for decision making, the whole system energy consumption is much more than 10−19, when counting the power to run the optical and electronic devices and including
that of emitted but undetected photons. To further reduce the total energy consumption will require additional replacement of electronics with optics.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit on their own energy claim in Section 4.
assertions.reader_inference: The sub-attojoule figure counts only the detected photon, so it is not a system-level energy comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state that the advantage is demonstrated in a specifically designed, narrowly purposed setting and that other AI tasks would need a carefully designed architecture to harvest quantum effects.
quotes: we would like to note that this advantage is demonstrated in a specificallydesigned, narrowly-purposed setting.
For other AI tasks, one would need to carefully design the architecture to harvest the power of quantum effects.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this scope limit in Section 4.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they demonstrated first photon machine learning with the entire network for image classification realized in optics on the detection of a single photon, call it the first unambiguous demonstration of quantum advantages for AI, and believe a hybrid quantum-classical system can establish practical advantages for realistic AI applications in the near term.
quotes: This is the first unambiguous demonstration of quantum advantages—in this case offered by the quantum superposition principle—for AI.
a hybrid quantum-classical system can establish practical advantages for realistic AI applications in near term.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion and belief; the near-term claim has no evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The priority and unambiguity claims depend on the 24.57% classical reference being the right comparator; the paper itself says the advantage is a statistical average in a narrow setting.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to date, there has not been a convincing experimental proof that quantum information science gives an edge to AI, and that earlier demonstrations inserting quantum elements into a neural network leave it unclear whether the improvement is material or achievable by better training.
quotes: hitherto there has not been a convincing experiment proof that QIS does give an edge to AI (8, 11).
it is unclear if such improvement is material or can be achieved alternatively by better training (6).
assertions.certainty_reason: A literature characterization by the authors, without a systematic review.

assertions.value: The authors state that benchmarking against a known performance ceiling established by rigorous mathematical proofs is difficult but important, that many quantum supremacy claims in time-to-solution have later been proven questionable or controversial, and that beating a known best does not necessarily prove a quantum advantage because better classical methods might be developed.
quotes: many claims of “quantum supremacy” in timeto-solution have been subsequently proven questionable or controversial (33–38).
Beating a known best does not necessarily prove a quantum advantage, as better classical methods might be developed in the future.
assertions.certainty_reason: The supremacy history is attributed to cited work; the rationale is the authors' argument.
assertions.reader_inference: This rationale applies to the paper's own classical reference, which is a bound for single-pixel detection from a cited derivation, not a bound over all classical strategies for the experiment as run.

assertions.value: The paper lists two authors with an affiliation at Quantum Computing Inc. in Hoboken, New Jersey, and states that there are no competing interests to declare.
quotes: Quantum Computing Inc., Hoboken, New Jersey
There are no competing interests to declare.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper metadata and a declaration.
assertions.reader_inference: The affiliation is recorded for provenance; the paper does not link the product of that company to the experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that the original data, more than 100 GB, and the codes will be uploaded to Google Drive, GitHub or another site, which indicates that the data and code were not yet available at the time of the paper.
quotes: The related original data (which is more than 100 GB) and codes will be uploaded on google drive, GitHub, or other website that allow such big file folder.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the availability of their own data in the declarations.
assertions.reader_inference: The 31.00% result cannot be reproduced from released data from this version of the paper.
